headline: High risk: shared shell/filesystem and broad orchestration surfaces make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading automation errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, and agent_b reads/writes files plus exposes many workflow I/O surfaces. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if A’s outputs are fed into B’s workflows or shared files. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF agent_a output is copied into agent_b workflow inputs or files, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF both agents share a workspace without content provenance checks, malicious instructions can traverse the pair.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of agent_a outputs into agent_b tasks.
Add a manual review step before B consumes A-generated files.
Use separate directories for each agent's artifacts.
Strip instructions from A outputs before passing them onward.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging and allowlist parsing for inter-agent messages.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and has network egress plus MCP; agent_b touches logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, database and cloud-storage data, and can write files. If they share a workspace or hand off files, sensitive material can flow from B into A’s broader I/O surfaces or out through A’s networked tools. The profiles do not show isolation strong enough to rule this out.
conditions: IF agent_b places database or cloud-storage data into shared files, agent_a can read it through MCP/stdin workflows.
IF agent_a forwards context or file contents through networked APIs, data from B may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep B’s sensitive inputs out of shared directories.
Restrict A’s network egress to the minimum allowlist.
Separate credentials and runtime identities for each agent.
Redact logs and artifacts before A can access them.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and DLP controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell and spawn subprocesses; agent_a can modify git state, while agent_b can write the filesystem and has elevated root/docker.sock requests. In a shared repo or directory, concurrent writes and git mutations can corrupt state or overwrite each other. Because both support multiple instances, the conflict is plausible in default orchestration unless locking is added.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or directory, concurrent writes can race.
IF agent_b receives root or docker.sock access while agent_a mutates git state, destructive conflicts become easier.
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate working tree.
Serialize git and filesystem writes with a lock.
Disable root/docker.sock for B unless required.
Assign distinct output paths per agent.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control and conflict detection.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a is positioned to generate analysis, prompts, or repository changes, and agent_b is an automation/orchestration system that can trigger HTTP, email, Slack, cloud, and queue actions. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, a mistaken or malicious A output can cascade into external side effects. The blast radius includes irreversible downstream actions, so this is high.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without verification, A’s errors can become automated actions.
IF A produces malformed facts or commands that B routes to email, Slack, or cloud tasks, downstream impact can propagate.
mitigations: Require human approval before B executes A-derived actions.
Validate A outputs against schemas before use.
Limit B to dry-run mode for A-originated tasks.
Log and diff A outputs before execution.
requires-engineering: add policy gates for high-impact workflow steps.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_b explicitly handles logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, database data, and cloud-storage data, while agent_a handles task prompts and repository metadata and can use network egress. The profiles do not state residency, retention, or certification alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through B’s workflows, retention and residency obligations may apply.
IF A forwards prompts or repository metadata into B’s external integrations, policy mismatches can occur.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent.
Block regulated data from shared workflows.
Review retention settings on B’s integrations.
Restrict A’s egress destinations.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls for both agents.
